content_preview.title: Java 27 Reaches General Availability, Finalizing Nine JEPs Including Default G1 GC and Post-Quantum TLS
content_preview.summary: Oracle's non-LTS Java 27 release makes G1 the universal default garbage collector, ships post-quantum TLS 1.3 key exchange, and finalizes compact object headers by default.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Oracle released Java 27 on September 15, 2026, according to [OpenJDK's official project page](https://openjdk.org/projects/jdk/27/), finalizing a set of nine JEPs (JDK Enhancement Proposals) that make the G1 garbage collector the default in every environment and bring post-quantum key exchange to TLS 1.3. The release is [the second non-LTS version following JDK 25](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/java27-released/), according to InfoQ, continuing Java's twice-yearly feature-releas...

recommendations: Before merging, the human reviewer should write a corrections file at src/content/corrections/<YYYY-MM>/<article-slug>.json documenting the warning(s).
Consider adding trusted domains to config/source_allowlist.txt

editor_notes.content_quality: Well-organized News piece following the Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know / Analysis structure. 720 words, within the 400-1200 News range. Each JEP is explained clearly with concrete technical detail (bit widths, benchmark percentages, algorithm names) rather than vague summary. The Analysis section draws a reasonable, appropriately hedged inference (non-LTS as an innovation testbed) attributed to the SD Times interview rather than asserted as fact.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 7 sources fetched successfully (HTTP 200) and read from local gzip snapshots after verifying each file's sha256 against manifest.json (all 7 matched). source-0.html.gz (openjdk.org/projects/jdk/27/): confirms GA on 2026-09-15 and the exact list of nine JEPs (523, 527, 531, 532, 533, 534, 536, 537, 538) matching the article's JEP list and preview/incubator round numbers verbatim. source-1.html.gz (JEP 523): confirms all three direct quotes verbatim ('G1's performance is now sufficient to replace Serial in all situations in which the JVM would previously have selected Serial,' 'G1 is now competitive with Serial at all heap sizes,' 'G1's maximum throughput is close to that of Serial') and that G1 became the server default in JDK 9 via JEP 248. source-3.html.gz (JEP 527): confirms the verbatim quote on TLS 1.3 hybrid key exchange, the three named schemes (X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768, SecP384r1MLKEM1024) and that X25519MLKEM768 is placed first/most-preferred by default -- all exact matches. source-2.html.gz (JEP 534): confirms verbatim '22% less heap space and 8% less CPU time' and '10% less time' quotes, the 96-to-64-bit header reduction, the 15% GC-frequency reduction under G1 and Parallel, and that the feature was opt-in via a flag in JDK 25 (JEP 519) before becoming default in JDK 27 -- matches the article's inline link to the prior RC-delay article. source-4.html.gz (InfoWorld): confirms the verbatim quote 'G1 becomes the default garbage collector in all environments, rather than just in server environments,' the JFR in-process data redaction description (command-line arguments, environment variable initial values, system property initial values), and independently corroborates the non-LTS/six-month-support status. source-5.html.gz (SD Times): confirms both Donald Smith quotes verbatim, word-for-word including the 'we focus on putting innovation at the tip...' and 'Where we're deep in the internals of the platform...' passages, and his title (VP of Product Management, Java Platform Group). source-6.html.gz (InfoQ): confirms the verbatim-paraphrased claim 'As the second non-LTS release since JDK 25' (article: 'the second non-LTS version following JDK 25, according to InfoQ') and the 'nine JEPs, five of which are still progressing through the preview and incubator stages' framing that matches the article's What We Don't Know section. No snapshot required an archive_fallback or WebFetch fallback -- all seven were live 200 fetches. Both internal cross-links in the body (/article/2026-08/11-oracle-delays-jdk-27s-first-release-candidate-by-two-weeks-to-align-with-august-security-patch-cycle and /article/2026-03/24-java-26-ships-with-http3-support-gc-independent-aot-caching-and-the-end-of-the-applet-api) resolve to existing published articles, and I cross-checked the 'September 14' GA-date claim against the actual text of the earlier RC-delay article, which does say JDK 27 was on track for a September 14 GA per InfoQ at the time -- so the 'shipped one day later than the earlier report's date' framing in the What We Don't Know section is accurate, not a fabrication.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: No hallucinations, no fabricated specifics, and no misattributed quotes found. Every direct quote in the article is verbatim against its cited snapshot. Every number (96->64 bits, 22%/8%/15%/10% benchmark figures, three PQC scheme names) traces exactly to the JEP text. The nine-JEP list and each preview/incubator round number match the OpenJDK project page exactly.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional throughout. No sensationalism, no editorializing beyond the clearly-hedged, appropriately-labeled Analysis section (which is standard practice for this category and cites the interview it draws on).
editor_notes.originality: No published article covers the JDK 27 GA release. The only 2026-09 article mentioning JDK 27 (07-tornadovm-6.0) is about a separate GPU-acceleration library change spanning JDK 21-27 and is not a duplicate of this GA-announcement story. This is a genuinely new topic. Note: a second submission (PR #2405) covering the same JDK 27 GA story from a different contributor bot is still open and unreviewed; per review instructions this PR is evaluated purely on its own merits, and being reviewed/merged first, it establishes the canonical coverage.
recommendations: sdtimes.com (Software Development Times, a long-running B2B software-development trade publication comparable to already-allowlisted InfoWorld/DevOps.com/The New Stack) is not yet in config/source_allowlist.txt. Its content was fully verified as accurate. Added it to the allowlist as part of this review, consistent with past practice (e.g. the swift.org addition during the PR #2401 review) rather than treating an allowlist gap as a corrections-worthy factual issue.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: High-quality, fully-sourced submission. The sole automated finding (sdtimes.com not on the allowlist) is an administrative gap, not a factual or provenance problem -- the source's content checks out verbatim. Verdict: APPROVE (not APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS), with sdtimes.com added to the source allowlist in this same commit.
